input_signals.name: Gambling For Resurrection Intensity
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(capx, ppent)), NEG(ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(re, at), 2))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Reinvestment relative to the installed capital base is value-destroying in proportion to how deep a firm's accumulated earnings deficit is, because equity holders of firms with large historical losses have convex payoffs and prefer risky expansion over debt repayment.
input_signals.reasoning: Replacing the hard INDICATOR with a winsorized, standardized retained-earnings-to-assets conditioner removes the degenerate zero mass and the reliance on a small negative-book-equity subsample: every firm now receives a continuous score and coverage matches capx and re availability. Centering at zero makes the interaction genuinely two-sided, so heavy investors with deep accumulated profits form the long leg and heavy investors with accumulated deficits form the short leg, while low-investment firms of either type sit near zero and do not drive the spread.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ratio( capx, ppent ) ), neg( zscore( winsor( ratio( re, at ), 2 ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Conjunctive Self-Funded Resilience
input_signals.expression: MIN(RANK(RATIO(SUB(oancf, capx), at)), RANK(RATIO(che, lct)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Financial resilience requires investment to be simultaneously self-funded and backstopped by liquid reserves; a firm scores high only if its operating cash flow covers its capital spending and its cash covers near-term obligations, and such firms are undervalued relative to their low refinancing risk.
input_signals.reasoning: MIN of the two ranks enforces the logical AND that the critic correctly noted SUMRANK does not deliver: a cash-rich firm that outspends its cash flow, or a self-funding firm with no liquidity, is capped at the low leg, so neither channel alone can produce a high score. It is also not merely the inverse of low investment, because a capital-intensive firm whose operating cash flow exceeds its capex still ranks highly, which separates the signal from CMA and from the short-side proposals in this set.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: min( rank( ratio( sub( oancf, capx ), at ) ), rank( ratio( che, lct ) ) )

input_signals.name: Headcount Expansion Without Earnings Cover
input_signals.expression: MIN(RANK(GROWTH(emp, 1)), RANK(NEG(RATIO(ib, lt))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Labor is the least reversible and most cash-hungry form of investment, so headcount expansion by firms whose earnings barely cover their obligations commits the firm to a fixed cost structure it cannot service, and the subsequent restructuring is not anticipated by investors focused on capital spending.
input_signals.reasoning: Employment growth is a real-quantity investment measure that appears in no FF5 factor and in no archive signal, and unlike capex it cannot be funded by depreciation or reversed by simply pausing a project. Conditioning on earnings-to-total-liabilities rather than on leverage keeps the fragility leg tied to debt-service capacity, so the top corner is specifically firms hiring into a coverage problem.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: min( rank( growth( emp, 1 ) ), rank( neg( ratio( ib, lt ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Validated Versus Unvalidated Expansion
input_signals.expression: SUB(MIN(RANK(DELTA(RATIO(sale, at), 1)), RANK(GROWTH(ppent, 1))), MIN(RANK(NEG(DELTA(RATIO(sale, at), 1))), RANK(GROWTH(ppent, 1))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Expansion is priced correctly only when the market can see whether it is being absorbed by demand: capacity growth accompanied by rising asset turnover is validated investment and should earn a premium, while identical capacity growth accompanied by falling turnover is unabsorbed capacity heading for write-downs.
input_signals.reasoning: This keeps the two-sided repair for the null-FMB problem but abandons the net-debt and cash-coverage constructs the critic identified, so the spread cannot collapse into a leverage-liquidity tilt: both corners share the same investment leg and differ only in the sign of the turnover change, making the signal a pure sign-flipping conditional that is near zero for non-investors. It therefore cannot be reproduced by CMA, which sorts on the level of growth without regard to whether output followed, and it uses only high-coverage annual items rather than the oancf-restricted sample.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: sub( min( rank( delta( ratio( sale, at ), 1 ) ), rank( growth( ppent, 1 ) ) ), min( rank( neg( delta( ratio( sale, at ), 1 ) ) ), rank( growth( ppent, 1 ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Smooth Funding Capacity Product
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(oancf, capx)), RANK(RATIO(che, lct)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Funding capacity for the investment program has two multiplicatively interacting dimensions — how many times over this year's operating cash flow covers this year's capital spending, and how much of the near-term obligation stack the cash stock can retire — and firms strong on both are the resilient investors the theme predicts.
input_signals.reasoning: The critic's algebra is correct that any symmetric difference of a conjunction and its complement collapses to the additive rank sum, so instead of a two-sided construction I change the operator geometry: the rank product is strictly increasing in both legs everywhere, whereas MIN has zero gradient in whichever leg is currently larger, which is the most plausible reason the archive's MIN slopes were flat while its decile spreads were significant. The self-funding leg is also re-specified as a scale-free coverage multiple rather than an asset-scaled difference, removing the size confound that a /at scaling introduces.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ratio( oancf, capx ) ), rank( ratio( che, lct ) ) )

input_signals.name: Flow-Only Coverage Of Committed Uses
input_signals.expression: RANK(RATIO(oancf, ADD(capx, dlc)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Recurring operating cash flow, not the accumulated cash pile, is what determines whether a firm can fund its capital program and roll its maturing debt without capital-market access; if so, coverage measured from the flow alone should carry the abnormal return and the cash stock is incidental.
input_signals.reasoning: This is the decisive diagnostic for the leading family, because every member so far mixes a stock leg (che) with a flow leg, leaving open the possibility that the alpha is the documented cash-holdings effect wearing an investment costume. Dropping the stock entirely gives a clean answer: if the alpha survives, the mechanism is genuinely investment-funding capacity and future refinements should build on flows; if it collapses, the archive's results are a liquidity-level premium and the search must be redirected.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: rank( ratio( oancf, add( capx, dlc ) ) )

input_signals.name: Coverage Premium Conditioned On Obligation Load
input_signals.expression: SUB(MIN(RANK(RATIO(oancf, ADD(capx, dlc))), RANK(RATIO(lt, at))), MIN(RANK(NEG(RATIO(oancf, ADD(capx, dlc)))), RANK(RATIO(lt, at))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Internal coverage of the capital program and maturing debt should be priced most strongly where the obligation load is heaviest, because that is where the marginal consequence of a funding shortfall is default rather than a postponed project; among firms with negligible liabilities the same coverage carries little information.
input_signals.reasoning: This construction eliminates the leverage main effect the critic identified: at median coverage the two MIN terms are identical for every leverage value, so the signal is exactly zero and cannot load on leverage per se, while the coverage ranking is amplified as the liability rank rises. It therefore tests the interaction claim itself rather than a leverage tilt, and unlike a ZSCORE-centered product it stays bounded and monotone in coverage, the property that has consistently separated signals with real FMB slopes from those with null slopes in this archive.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: sub( min( rank( ratio( oancf, add( capx, dlc ) ) ), rank( ratio( lt, at ) ) ), min( rank( neg( ratio( oancf, add( capx, dlc ) ) ) ), rank( ratio( lt, at ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Conjunctive Coverage Of Investment And Claims
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(MA(ib, 3), capx), lt)), RANK(RATIO(che, ADD(lct, capx))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Resilience requires both a sustainable earnings surplus after investment relative to total obligations and a cash stock large enough to cover near-term claims *including* the coming year's capital program; firms strong on both dimensions are those for which no shock forces external financing.
input_signals.reasoning: This settles the operator question at full coverage: the additive smooth ratios produce alphas with weak slopes while rank conjunctions reorder firms in a way that has repeatedly lifted FMB t-stats above 3.5, and here both legs come from the highest-coverage inputs so the test is not confounded by sample size. Adding capx to the denominator of the liquidity leg is also a substantive improvement over the archived che/lct, since it makes the liquidity requirement depend on the firm's own investment commitment rather than on obligations alone.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ratio( sub( ma( ib, 3 ), capx ), lt ) ), rank( ratio( che, add( lct, capx ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Coverage Gap Amplified By Short Maturity Reliance
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(NEG(RATIO(SUB(SUB(ib, DELTA(wcap, 1)), capx), lt))), RANK(RATIO(dlc, ADD(dltt, dlc))))
input_signals.hypothesis: A funding shortfall becomes a distress event only when the claims come due soon: firms whose cash earnings fail to cover their capital program are vulnerable in proportion to how much of their debt sits at the short end of the maturity structure and therefore must be renegotiated immediately.
input_signals.reasoning: This gives the short side the same economic content as the family's successful long side while conditioning on maturity structure rather than on leverage level, so the timing of refinancing — not the amount of debt — supplies the amplification, an axis the archive has never tested. Both legs are monotone ranks computed from full-coverage inputs, and the shortfall leg is the exact mirror of Signal 1, which lets us verify whether the family's information is symmetric across tails or concentrated on the resilient side as the MIN-based results suggest.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( neg( ratio( sub( sub( ib, delta( wcap, 1 ) ), capx ), lt ) ) ), rank( ratio( dlc, add( dltt, dlc ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Funding Capacity At Its Own Historical Low
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(ib, capx), lt)), TS_RANK(RATIO(SUB(ib, capx), lt), 5))
input_signals.hypothesis: Cross-sectional funding capacity is contaminated by permanent industry differences in capital intensity, so what identifies a firm sliding toward strain is being simultaneously low against peers *and* at the bottom of its own five-year range; conversely, a firm at a personal high in coverage is being re-rated upward, and the market adjusts slowly.
input_signals.reasoning: This replaces the rejected input substitution with a genuinely new dimension the archive has never used — position within a firm's *own* history of funding capacity, which is immune to the industry-level heterogeneity that makes pooled ranks of capital-intensity ratios hard to interpret. The conjunction of level and own-history position means neither a permanently strong firm nor a temporarily improving weak firm scores at the extremes, so the signal isolates firms whose funding capacity is both absolutely and relatively deteriorating.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ratio( sub( ib, capx ), lt ) ), ts_rank( ratio( sub( ib, capx ), lt ), 5 ) )

input_signals.name: Surplus After Investment And Maturing Debt
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(MA(ib, 3), ADD(MA(capx, 3), dlc)), lt)), RANK(RATIO(che, ADD(lct, MA(capx, 3)))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Committed uses of cash comprise both the capital program and the debt that matures within the year, so the earnings surplus that matters for resilience is what remains after funding investment *and* retiring short-term debt, measured against the total obligation stack.
input_signals.reasoning: Every archive member that placed maturing debt alongside capex in committed uses produced the largest alphas (+7.4%, +7.2%), but all were confined to the `oancf` sample, so this tests whether that ingredient survives at full coverage inside the conjunctive structure that supplies the FMB slope. If it does, the family's best version combines the alpha-generating definition of committed uses with the slope-generating operator geometry, which is the natural end point of this line of search.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ratio( sub( ma( ib, 3 ), add( ma( capx, 3 ), dlc ) ), lt ) ), rank( ratio( che, add( lct, ma( capx, 3 ) ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Coverage Level Times Self-Funding Habit
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(MA(ib, 3), capx), lt)), RANK(MA(INDICATOR(SUB(ib, capx), 0), 5)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Resilience requires both a currently adequate surplus after investment and a demonstrated habit of funding capital spending internally; a firm that has earned more than it invested in most of the last five years has revealed a business model that does not require capital markets, whereas one good year of surplus at a habitually externally-financed firm is not informative.
input_signals.reasoning: The second leg is a *frequency* statistic — the fraction of the last five years in which earnings exceeded capital spending — which is a genuinely different measurement of the same economic condition than a magnitude, so unlike the rejected version the two legs are not the same variable rescaled and can diverge sharply for lumpy investors and cyclical firms. Loss-frequency conditioning of this type produced the archive's only chronicity evidence, and applying it to funding rather than to profitability keeps the signal inside the investment-distress interaction rather than reducing to a profitability sort.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ratio( sub( ma( ib, 3 ), capx ), lt ) ), rank( ma( indicator( sub( ib, capx ), 0 ), 5 ) ) )

input_signals.name: Funding Surplus Per Unit Of Earnings Risk
input_signals.expression: RANK(RATIO(RATIO(SUB(MA(ib, 3), capx), lt), VOL(RATIO(ib, at), 5)))
input_signals.hypothesis: A given surplus after investment buys very different protection depending on how volatile the earnings stream is: a surplus equal to two percent of obligations is comfortable when return on assets moves by one point a year and worthless when it moves by ten, so the priced quantity is the number of earnings shocks the firm can absorb while still funding its capital program.
input_signals.reasoning: This replaces the rejected smoothing knob with a distance-to-distress construction — surplus scaled by the standard deviation of the shock that threatens it — which is the structural form used by bankruptcy models and which no archive signal has employed, since earnings volatility previously entered only as a multiplicative conditioner and failed. Scaling rather than multiplying is the economically correct use of a second moment here, and it should sharpen both tails: capital-intensive stable firms rise and volatile marginal investors fall, which is precisely the ordering the coverage family currently gets only partially right.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: rank( ratio( ratio( sub( ma( ib, 3 ), capx ), lt ), vol( ratio( ib, at ), 5 ) ) )

input_signals.name: Realized Cash And Sustainable Earnings Complements
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ADD(oancf, che), ADD(capx, dlc))), RANK(RATIO(SUB(MA(ib, 3), capx), lt)))
input_signals.hypothesis: This year's realized cash resources against committed uses and the three-year sustainable earnings surplus against total obligations answer different questions — can the firm pay now, and can it keep paying — and firms that satisfy both are more resilient than either measure alone indicates.
input_signals.reasoning: These are the archive's highest-alpha construct (+7.4%, t 4.48, but fmb 1.24) and its highest-slope construct (fmb 4.41), and they have never been combined; because the first is a current-year cash ratio and the second a multi-year accrual surplus scaled by a different denominator, the product is not a rescaling of either. The cost is the 0.089 `oancf` sample, which makes this the natural counterpart to Signal 1: together they show whether the full-coverage backfill or the restricted-sample combination is the better route to a high alpha with a reliable slope.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ratio( add( oancf, che ), add( capx, dlc ) ) ), rank( ratio( sub( ma( ib, 3 ), capx ), lt ) ) )

input_signals.name: Coverage Level Times Coverage Improvement
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(MA(ib, 3), capx), lt)), RANK(DELTA(RATIO(SUB(ib, capx), lt), 1)))
input_signals.hypothesis: A strong funding position that is still improving signals a firm moving away from any need for external capital, whereas the same level in deterioration is a firm on its way into the strained corner; the market extrapolates the level and underreacts to the direction.
input_signals.reasoning: Every coverage signal in the archive is a level or a smoothed level, so the trajectory dimension is untested inside the family that actually works, and it is economically distinct because the change is dominated by the most recent year while the three-year average deliberately suppresses it. Unlike the frequency and volatility enrichments that destroyed alpha by discarding magnitude, this leg preserves a continuous magnitude ordering, which is the property those failures suggest matters.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ratio( sub( ma( ib, 3 ), capx ), lt ) ), rank( delta( ratio( sub( ib, capx ), lt ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: Triple Channel Coverage Conjunction
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(MA(ib, 3), capx), lt)), MUL(RANK(RATIO(che, ADD(lct, capx))), RANK(RATIO(SUB(act, lct), ADD(TS_SUM(capx, 3), dlc)))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Three complementary conditions — a sustainable earnings surplus after investment, a cash stock covering near-term claims plus the capital program, and net working capital covering the multi-year program plus maturing debt — must all hold for a firm to be immune to financing shocks, and requiring all three concentrates the extreme portfolios on genuinely unconstrained firms.
input_signals.reasoning: The additive version of exactly these three channels earned α 4.2% with fmb 1.64 while the two-channel product earned α 5.0% with fmb 4.41, which implies the aggregation rule matters more than the number of channels; this test separates those two effects by holding the channels fixed and switching averaging for multiplication. Each of the three legs has independently produced an alpha above 4% in this archive, so a null result here would be strong evidence that two conditions already exhaust the information.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ratio( sub( ma( ib, 3 ), capx ), lt ) ), mul( rank( ratio( che, add( lct, capx ) ) ), rank( ratio( sub( act, lct ), add( ts_sum( capx, 3 ), dlc ) ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Retained Funds Surplus Conjunction
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(DELTA(re, 1), capx), lt)), RANK(RATIO(che, ADD(lct, capx))))
input_signals.hypothesis: The funds genuinely available to carry an investment program are the earnings the firm actually retains after honouring its dividend commitments, so the surplus that matters is the annual increment to retained earnings net of capital spending, measured against total obligations.
input_signals.reasoning: This abandons the biased cash-flow reconstruction entirely — no depreciation term is needed and no observation is backfilled, so the pooled rank cannot proxy for the missing-statement subsample — and replaces it with a quantity the archive has never used in the coverage family: the change in retained earnings, which is income after the dividend claim that a distressed firm can only cut at a reputational cost. Because dividend-paying and non-paying firms with identical earnings receive different scores, the leg is economically distinct from every ib-based surplus already tested, while retaining full sample coverage.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ratio( sub( delta( re, 1 ), capx ), lt ) ), rank( ratio( che, add( lct, capx ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Cash Runway Against The Capital Program
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(MA(ib, 3), capx), lt)), RANK(RATIO(che, TS_SUM(capx, 3))))
input_signals.hypothesis: The liquidity question posed by the investment-distress interaction is not whether cash covers the liability stack but how many years of the firm's own capital program the cash stock could fund unaided; a firm holding three years of programme spending in cash can complete its projects through any financing freeze.
input_signals.reasoning: Rather than relabelling `dlc` between numerator and denominator, this replaces the solvency-style liquidity leg with a pure runway measure defined solely against the firm's own investment commitment, which is the interaction the theme actually specifies and which is far less collinear with the archived `che/lct` and `che/(lct+capx)` legs than a net-cash variant would be. Using the cumulative three-year program as the yardstick also removes the single-year capex lumpiness that makes one-year runway measures noisy, and both inputs are high-coverage items.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ratio( sub( ma( ib, 3 ), capx ), lt ) ), rank( ratio( che, ts_sum( capx, 3 ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Restraint Against Own Investment Norm
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(NEG(RATIO(capx, MA(capx, 5)))), RANK(RATIO(ib, lt)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Aggressive or disciplined investment is only meaningful relative to what a firm normally spends, so a capital budget running below its own five-year norm at a firm with solid earnings coverage reveals deliberate restraint by a management team that could afford to spend, which is the resilience the theme predicts.
input_signals.reasoning: Every investment leg in this archive benchmarks capex against assets, plant, or the cross-section, never against the firm's own history, so within-firm abnormal investment is the one untested measurement of the "aggressive versus disciplined" distinction and it is immune to the industry capital-intensity problem that motivates Signal 1. Pairing it with earnings coverage rather than liquidity keeps the interaction squarely on the discipline-versus-strain axis and separates voluntary restraint from the forced contraction that the archive has already shown earns negative alpha.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( neg( ratio( capx, ma( capx, 5 ) ) ) ), rank( ratio( ib, lt ) ) )

input_signals.name: Surplus Against Contractual Claims Only
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(MA(ib, 3), capx), ADD(dltt, lct))), RANK(RATIO(che, TS_SUM(capx, 3))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Total liabilities is the wrong denominator for distress because it bundles deferred taxes, pension and other accounting provisions that never trigger a default; the claims that can force a firm into restructuring are long-term debt and the obligations due within the year, and coverage should be measured against those alone.
input_signals.reasoning: This is an economic re-definition of what a claim *is*, not a benchmark swap: it changes which firms are classified as heavily obligated — capital-intensive firms with large deferred tax balances move up, firms with genuine bank and bond debt move down — and that reclassification is the whole content of the test. Pairing it with the runway leg rather than the claims-based liquidity leg also removes the `lct` term from both sides of the conjunction, so the two legs share no variable and the product is not a near-rescale of any evaluated signal.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ratio( sub( ma( ib, 3 ), capx ), add( dltt, lct ) ) ), rank( ratio( che, ts_sum( capx, 3 ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Accounting Consistent Net Investment Surplus
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(MA(ib, 3), DELTA(ppent, 1)), lt)), RANK(RATIO(che, ADD(lct, capx))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Earnings are already net of depreciation, so subtracting gross capital spending double-counts the maintenance of the existing asset base; the funds genuinely consumed by expansion are the increase in net plant, and a firm whose earnings exceed that increment is self-funding its growth.
input_signals.reasoning: This repairs the one measurement flaw the critic identified twice and that I never addressed — the depreciation mismatch between `ib` and `capx`, which mechanically penalises utilities, transports and other high-depreciation industries regardless of their true funding position. The change is economic rather than cosmetic because it reclassifies every capital-intensive firm that is merely replacing worn-out plant from "strained investor" to "self-funding", and it needs only full-coverage balance-sheet items.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ratio( sub( ma( ib, 3 ), delta( ppent, 1 ) ), lt ) ), rank( ratio( che, add( lct, capx ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Quick Asset Coverage Conjunction
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(MA(ib, 3), capx), lt)), RANK(RATIO(SUB(act, invt), ADD(lct, capx))))
input_signals.hypothesis: The liquid resources that can actually meet near-term claims and fund a capital program are cash and receivables; inventory is slow, discounted when sold under pressure, and often the very thing accumulating when a business deteriorates, so it should be excluded from the buffer.
input_signals.reasoning: The archive has now bracketed this question — cash alone delivered α 5.0% while total non-cash working capital delivered only 3.1% — but the intermediate and economically correct measure, quick assets, has never been tested, and receivables are a large near-cash resource that the cash-only leg discards entirely. Excluding inventory also removes the one current-asset component whose growth is a documented *warning* sign, so this leg should be cleaner as well as broader than either extreme.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ratio( sub( ma( ib, 3 ), capx ), lt ) ), rank( ratio( sub( act, invt ), add( lct, capx ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Consistent Surplus With Quick Liquidity
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(MA(ib, 3), DELTA(ppent, 1)), lt)), RANK(RATIO(SUB(act, invt), ADD(lct, capx))))
input_signals.hypothesis: A firm is resilient when its sustained earnings cover the net expansion of its asset base relative to obligations and its cash and receivables cover near-term claims plus the capital program — the two funding conditions stated with internally consistent accounting on both sides.
input_signals.reasoning: This is the synthesis candidate for the family: it applies the depreciation repair to the flow leg and the quick-asset repair to the stock leg simultaneously, so if each fix helps individually this should be the strongest member, and if it matches rather than beats them we learn the two corrections address the same underlying noise. Coverage remains near the family maximum because every input is a standard balance-sheet or income item.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ratio( sub( ma( ib, 3 ), delta( ppent, 1 ) ), lt ) ), rank( ratio( sub( act, invt ), add( lct, capx ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Total Outlay Coverage On Both Legs
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(MA(ib, 3), MA(ADD(capx, COALESCE(aqc, 0)), 3)), lt)), RANK(RATIO(che, ADD(lct, MA(ADD(capx, COALESCE(aqc, 0)), 3)))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Investment is the sum of what a firm builds and what it buys, so both the surplus test and the required-liquidity test must be measured against total investment outlay averaged over the program horizon rather than against a single year of organic capital expenditure.
input_signals.reasoning: This fixes the internal inconsistency the critic identified: total outlay now appears in both legs, and averaging it over three years matches the horizon of the earnings average, so lumpy one-off acquisitions no longer collide with a smoothed numerator. The economic content is a redefinition of what "investing" means for the whole family — serial acquirers, who are precisely the aggressive expanders the theme targets, are currently scored as if they invested nothing beyond plant.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ratio( sub( ma( ib, 3 ), ma( add( capx, coalesce( aqc, 0 ) ), 3 ) ), lt ) ), rank( ratio( che, add( lct, ma( add( capx, coalesce( aqc, 0 ) ), 3 ) ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Liquidity Sized To Peak Commitment
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(MA(ib, 3), capx), lt)), RANK(RATIO(SUB(act, invt), ADD(lct, TS_MAX(capx, 5)))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Capital programs are lumpy, so the buffer a firm needs is set by its heaviest spending year rather than by an average: quick assets that comfortably cover near-term claims plus the largest annual outlay of the past five years mean the firm can absorb its own peak commitment without external funding.
input_signals.reasoning: This drops the smoothing ablation whose coverage rationale the critic correctly showed to be wrong, and replaces it with an untested economic claim about the shape rather than the level of the investment program — a firm spending 5% of assets every year and one alternating between 1% and 12% require very different buffers, yet every liquidity denominator tested so far treats them identically. Using the five-year maximum makes the required-buffer benchmark firm-specific and forward-looking in the sense that matters for a financing freeze, and all inputs remain full-coverage annual items.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ratio( sub( ma( ib, 3 ), capx ), lt ) ), rank( ratio( sub( act, invt ), add( lct, ts_max( capx, 5 ) ) ) ) )
